children.name: Hydrochoerus
children.description: Capybaras — the world's largest rodents, semi-aquatic grazers of South American rivers, lakes, and marshes. A large male can weigh 66 kg. Capybaras are highly social, living in groups of 10–20 that may swell to hundreds during the dry season around shrinking water bodies. They are excellent swimmers and can remain submerged for up to five minutes to evade predators. Their eyes, ears, and nostrils are positioned high on the head, allowing them to monitor their surroundings while almost completely submerged. Jaguars, anacondas, caimans, pumas, and harpy eagles all prey on capybaras, making them a keystone prey species across South American wetlands.

children.name: Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris
children.description: The capybara or greater capybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris) is the largest living rodent, native to all countries in South America except Chile.

children.name: Hydrochoerus isthmius
children.description: The lesser capybara is a large semi-aquatic rodent found in South America that has vast similarities with, yet subtle differences from, the slightly larger common capybara, the largest species of rodent in the world.

children.name: Cavia
children.description: Guinea pigs — small, stout rodents of the Andes, domesticated by Andean peoples at least 5,000 years ago for food and still a dietary staple in Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador. Guinea pigs (called 'cuy') are more efficient at converting plant matter to protein than cattle, and they produce no greenhouse gases. Domestic guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus) descend from wild species still found in the Andes and differ significantly from their wild ancestors in coat colour, body size, and behaviour. Wild guinea pigs are shy and cryptic; domestic ones are placid and tolerant of handling.

children.name: Cavia porcellus
children.description: The guinea pig or domestic guinea pig (Cavia porcellus), also known as the cavy or domestic cavy ( ), is a species of rodent belonging to the genus Cavia, family Caviidae.

children.name: American
children.description:
Guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus), also known as cavies, have been domesticated since, leading to the development of a diverse array of breeds.
As with most domesticated animals, guinea pig breeds exhibit a wide range of physical characteristics and serve various purposes. Some are show breeds, notable for their long, flowing hair, while others are laboratory breeds, used as model organisms in scientific research.

children.name: Abyssinian
children.description: The Abyssinian is a breed of guinea pig that is relatively common as both a pet and show animal. The Abyssinian is set apart from other breeds of guinea pig by its coat, which is marked with radially growing swirls or cowlicks of hair referred to as rosettes.

children.name: Teddy
children.description:
Guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus), also known as cavies, have been domesticated since, leading to the development of a diverse array of breeds.
As with most domesticated animals, guinea pig breeds exhibit a wide range of physical characteristics and serve various purposes. Some are show breeds, notable for their long, flowing hair, while others are laboratory breeds, used as model organisms in scientific research.

children.name: Rex
children.description: A Rex is a breed of guinea pig known for its short, dense, and very coarse wiry fur that stands upright, giving it a somewhat hedgehog-like appearance. They are popular pets due to their calm, gentle temperament and low maintenance grooming needs, as their fur doesn't require frequent brushing like some other guinea pig breeds.

children.name: Peruvian
children.description: The Peruvian, formerly the Angora, is a Spanish breed of guinea pig.

children.name: Silkie
children.description:
The Silkie breed, also called Sheltie in the United Kingdom, originated in the United Kingdom during the 1970s from a crossbreed between a Peruvian and an American Shorthair.
They are understood to generally have a tamer personality than most other guinea pig breeds.

children.name: Texel
children.description:
Guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus), also known as cavies, have been domesticated since, leading to the development of a diverse array of breeds.
As with most domesticated animals, guinea pig breeds exhibit a wide range of physical characteristics and serve various purposes. Some are show breeds, notable for their long, flowing hair, while others are laboratory breeds, used as model organisms in scientific research.

children.name: Coronet
children.description: The Coronet resembles the Silkie with its smooth coat growing backward over its body, but it has a crest on its forehead. As with the short-coated crested breeds, this crest should be symmetrical and distinct with a small centre and no sticking hairs. The ears of a coronet may also droop sightly.

children.name: White Crested
children.description: The White Crested is similar to the American, but they have one white rosette on the forehead. The breed standards and ideals are nearly identical, with the exception that a White Crested cavy's crest should be completely of a color different from the rest of the animal. Most usually the crest is white, as necessitated by the ACBA standard. No other white hair should be present in the animal. By this standard, White Cresteds are not bred in colorations that have white anywhere on the body, such as Dutch, roan, and Dalmatian.

children.name: American Crested
children.description: The American Crested is a short-haired guinea pig with a distinctive crest of hair on the top of its head that is a different color than the rest of its body.

children.name: Skinny Pig
children.description: The Skinny Pig or Skinny is an almost hairless strain of guinea pig. Skinny pigs typically have hair on their muzzles, feet, and legs, but are hairless over the remainder of their bodies. Some of them have a thin covering of fuzzy hair on their backs as well. The Skinny guinea pig is not one of the 13 recognized cavy breeds by the American Cavy Breeders Association. A healthy skinny has skin that is mostly smooth, with some wrinkling around the legs and neck. The body is full with no appearance of spine or ribs. Skinnies can come in a variety of skin colors and patterns, including "Dutch", "Brindle", and "Himalayan". The term skinny is used for hairless guinea pigs either because it colloquially refers to the exposed skin of the animal, or because it describes their thinner appearance due to their lack of hair.

children.name: Baldwin
children.description:
The Baldwin guinea pig is a breed developed from a spontaneous genetic mutation in Carol Miller's show-line of white crested golden agouti. Though born fully furred, Baldwin guinea pigs begin to lose their fur at two to five days of age, starting at the nose and leaving them almost entirely hairless by about two months of age. They retain whiskers and sometimes a few hairs on their feet.
Baldwins are known for having skin of a rubbery texture, many wrinkles and large, droopy ears. They come in all colors and patterns that haired guinea pigs come, such as Dutch, tortoiseshell, broken colors, Himalayan and selfs.

children.name: Cavia aperea
children.description: The Brazilian guinea pig (Cavia aperea) (preá in Portuguese) is a wild guinea pig species found in Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Paraguay, Uruguay and Venezuela..

children.name: Cavia tschudii
children.description: The montane guinea pig (Cavia tschudii) is a species of caviid rodent found in the Andes in South America..

children.name: Cavia fulgida
children.description: The shiny guinea pig (Cavia fulgida) is a guinea pig species of southeastern South America..

children.name: Cavia magna
children.description: Cavia magna, commonly known as the greater guinea pig, is a species of rodent in the family Caviidae, native to South America..

children.name: Cavia intermedia
children.description: Santa Catarina's guinea pig (Cavia intermedia) or Moleques do Sul cavy is a rare guinea pig species of southeastern South America..

children.name: Dolichotis
children.description: Maras (Patagonian cavies) — large, long-legged guinea pig relatives that are among the most unusual rodents on Earth. With their long ears, hare-like legs, and swift bounding gait, they bear a striking resemblance to small deer or jackrabbits, a classic example of convergent evolution. Maras are unusual among rodents in forming long-term monogamous pairs; a male will follow his female closely and drive away rival males. They use a communal crèche system where multiple pairs deposit their young in a shared burrow tended by a rotating group of adults.

children.name: Dolichotis patagonum
children.description: The Patagonian mara (Dolichotis patagonum) is a rodent in the mara genus Dolichotis.

children.name: Dolichotis salinicola
children.description: The Chacoan mara (Dolichotis salinicola) or Chacoan cavy is a relatively large South American rodent of the cavy family.

children.name: Kerodon
children.description: Rock cavies — unique among caviids for their arboreal and rock- dwelling habits, found in the dry, rocky outcrops (lajeiros) of the Brazilian caatinga and cerrado. They are agile climbers, leaping confidently among boulders with the help of small, padded feet. Unlike most caviids, rock cavies are not grazers but specialized browsers on leaves, bark, and seeds.

children.name: Kerodon rupestris
children.description: The rock cavy or mocó (Kerodon rupestris) is a species of cavy that is endemic to eastern Brazil.

children.name: Kerodon acrobata
children.description: The acrobatic cavy (Kerodon acrobata) also known as the acrobatic moco and climbing cavy is a cavy species native to Brazil.

children.name: Galea
children.description: Yellow-toothed cavies — smaller, more gracile relatives of guinea pigs with distinctive yellow-orange enamel on their incisors. They inhabit open grasslands, scrub, and rocky slopes across a wide range of South America, from the Andes to the Atlantic coast. Socially they are unusual among caviids: they live in groups with a dominance hierarchy but lack the strong monogamous pair bonds seen in maras.

children.name: Galea musteloides
children.description: The common yellow-toothed cavy (Galea musteloides) is a species of rodent in the family Caviidae, closely related to the domesticated guinea pig..

children.name: Galea spixii
children.description: Spix's yellow-toothed cavy (Galea spixii) is a rodent, a cavy species from South America..

children.name: Galea flavidens
children.description: The Brazilian yellow-toothed cavy (Galea flavidens) is a cavy species from South America..

children.name: Galea leucoblephara
children.description: Galea leucoblephara, commonly known as the lowland yellow-toothed cavy, is a species of rodent in the family Caviidae..

children.name: Microcavia
children.description: Mountain cavies — the smallest members of the guinea pig family, adapted to arid and high-altitude environments in the southern Andes and Patagonia. They are social, diurnal rodents that live in burrow systems and feed on grasses, leaves, and seeds. Their compact size and efficient water metabolism allow them to thrive in some of the driest habitats on the continent.

children.name: Microcavia australis
children.description: The southern mountain cavy (Microcavia australis) is a species of South American rodent in the family Caviidae..

children.name: Microcavia niata
children.description: The Andean mountain cavy (Microcavia niata) is a species of rodent in the family Caviidae..
